source.title: Scaling Laws for Gradient Descent and Sign Descent for Linear Bigram Models under Zipf's Law

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws but its results concern optimization convergence in a linear bigram model with squared loss, not the held-out cross-entropy scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation specified by the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports loss-convergence results for gradient descent and sign descent versus iteration count and vocabulary dimension, including a real-data check. These use squared training loss and do not test the claim versions' held-out pretraining cross-entropy or parameter/token/compute scaling. Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are cited as related work; their findings are not the paper's results.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and numerically checks optimization-time scaling, meaning iterations to a relative squared training-loss error, for GD and sign descent on a linear bigram quadratic as vocabulary size d grows. It reports no held-out cross-entropy of language models versus parameters, tokens or compute. It reports no extrapolation, compute-optimal split, architecture-shape, other-modality or downstream results. Its remark that the (1/ε)^p form is specific to α>1 concerns convergence of a convex quadratic, not fitted LM loss laws. So it does not test V7 or any other version. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that the usual (1/ε)^p scaling form holds only for α>1, and may miss strong dimension dependence when vocabulary size is scaled. They suggest longer training may be needed for larger vocabularies. As limitations they list the online setting, momentum, cross-entropy loss, more complex models and finite-d corrections.
record.recipe_differences: The paper derives deterministic optimization-convergence results for gradient descent and sign descent on a linear bigram model with squared loss, rather than measuring held-out cross-entropy in large language-model training runs.
record.method_sensitivity: The results depend on the frequency exponent α and optimizer. Sign-descent analysis uses a simplified model of oscillations and a step-size selected for the training horizon; on OpenWebText the sign-descent step-size is numerically optimized.

fits_no_version.finding: On a linear bigram squared-loss model with Zipf (α=1) frequencies, iterations to reach relative training error ε scale as d^(1−ε) for GD and about d^(1/2) for tuned sign descent. OpenWebText-derived dynamics match these predictions qualitatively. For α>1, GD follows the familiar (1/ε)^p form; for α≤1 the form differs and depends on d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization time versus vocabulary size on heavy-tailed token data depends on the optimizer and the tail exponent; sign descent scales better than GD for Zipfian data.

record.problems: The analysis concerns a simplified linear bigram model and squared loss, not cross-entropy training of large language models. Sign-descent theory relies on an assumption that averages its oscillations. The authors note that finite-dimensional convergence to the asymptotic regime can be slow, especially for α = 1.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for other frequency-exponent regimes or the paper's illustrative and auxiliary analyses; these do not test the claim versions. Figure 1 and Figures 4–7 illustrate optimization dynamics or asymptotic scaling, while Appendices B–E analyze optimization rates and proofs.

untested.parts: Held-out LM pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute; the paper measures only training-loss convergence in iterations on a linear squared-loss model.
Extrapolation from small to large runs.
Depth/width/shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Dependence of fitted LM loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices; the paper's functional-form remarks concern optimization rates of a quadratic, not fitted LM laws.

record.verdict_notes: Rows correctly linked to none. Their states are cannot_determine because they measure a different construct (optimization iterations vs dimension on a quadratic). This is not LM held-out loss scaling. No verdict labels are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from smaller language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Effects of architecture details such as depth and width at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance scaling or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and bending of those curves.
